title: The WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology on sputum sample, bronchial washing (BW), and bronchial brushing (BB): implied risk of malignancy (ROM) and clinical management options by diagnostic category
tablehtml:
Diagnostic category

Estimated ROMa

Clinical management optionsb

"Insufficient/Inadequate/Non-diagnostic"

Sputum sample: 0–100%

BW: 38–81%

BB: 0–75%

Consider repeating the sampling or use BB/BW (in case of sputum sample) and/or FNAB, depending on CLIN-IMG-MICRO

"Benign"

Sputum sample: 0–42%

BW: 38–42%

BB: 32–38%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO; if these confirm a benign diagnosis, then routine follow-up at 3–6 months; if no correlation, consider new sampling

"Atypical"

Sputum sample: 86–100%

BW: 62–86%

BB: 79–100%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO; if these are “Benign”, repeat; if “Atypical” or “Suspicious for malignancy”, perform BB/BW or FNAB with or without CNB

"Suspicious for malignancy"

Sputum sample: 100%

BW: 83–100%

BB: 75–100%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO, and perform BB/BW or FNAB with or without CNB; these cases need to be discussed at MDT meetings

"Malignant"

Sputum sample: 100%

BW: 98–100%

BB: 94–100%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO, and perform BB/BW or FNAB with or without CNB to confirm diagnosis before definitive treatment

CLIN-IMG-MICRO, clinical, imaging, and microbiological findings; CNB, core needle biopsy, including endobronchial biopsy; FNAB, fine-needle aspiration biopsy, including endobronchial ultrasound–guided and transthoracic FNAB; MDT, multidisciplinary team.

aEstimated ROMs are based on few retrospective studies {30051969; 34319004}. For some types of sampling, the number of cases studied is low. Prospective studies are strongly recommended in this field. bManagement options for patients with lung lesions may depend on a variety of factors, including clinical and imaging characteristics, the site of the lesion, the risk of carcinoma of the lung, local disease prevalence, and the local medical infrastructure available. Some clinical management suggestions are outlined above. In medically poorly resourced settings, an “Insufficient”, “Atypical”, or “Suspicious for malignancy” sputum sample report after correlation with imaging such as a CXR would usually be repeated and the slides reviewed if BB, BW, and endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial FNAB are not available. Similarly, if BB and BW were “Insufficient”, “Atypical”, or “Suspicious for malignancy” a repeat BW and BB procedure would be recommended after correlation with imaging if endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial FNAB is not available.

Recommendations:

1. When repeating a sputum sample, always provide clear instructions regarding the procedure or assist the patient with a physiotherapist or trained paramedic.

2. Whenever a sputum sample, BW/BB, or FNAB result is received, correlation with clinical, imaging, and microbiological findings is mandatory; in patients suspected of having a malignancy, this will ideally be carried out in a multidisciplinary meeting.

3. Whenever an “Atypical” or “Suspicious for malignancy” report is provided, or whenever there is discrepancy between the clinical, imaging, and microbiological findings and the cytopathology report, the reporting cytopathologist should, if possible, get a second expert opinion on the cytopathology.

4. Routine follow-up at 3–6 months for “Benign” and “Atypical” reports is determined by the patient’s lung cancer risk.

title: The WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology on FNAB: implied risk of malignancy (ROM) and clinical management options by diagnostic category
tablehtml:
Diagnostic category

Estimated ROMa

Clinical management optionsb

"Insufficient/Inadequate/Non-diagnostic"

43–53%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO, ideally discuss at an MDT meeting, and perform repeat FNAB with or without CNB

"Benign"

19–64%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO; if these confirm a benign diagnosis, then routine follow-up at 3–6 months; if no correlation, perform repeat FNAB with or without CNB

"Atypical"

46–55%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO, and ideally discuss at an MDT meeting; if all show a benign diagnosis, then routine follow-up at 3–6 months; if no correlation, perform repeat FNAB with ROSE with or without CNB

"Suspicious for malignancy"

75–88%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO, and ideally discuss at an MDT meeting; if all four support a diagnosis of malignancy, consider definitive treatment; if no correlation that lesion is malignant, perform repeat FNAB with ROSE with or without CNB

"Malignant"

87–100%

Correlate with CLIN-IMG-MICRO, and ideally discuss at an MDT meeting; if all four support a diagnosis of malignancy, provide definitive treatment; if no correlation that lesion is malignant, consider repeat FNAB with ROSE with or without CNB

CLIN-IMG-MICRO, clinical, imaging, and microbiological findings; CNB, core needle biopsy, including endobronchial biopsy; FNAB, fine-needle aspiration biopsy, including endobronchial ultrasound–guided and transthoracic FNAB; MDT, multidisciplinary team; ROSE, rapid onsite evaluation.

aEstimated ROMs are based on few retrospective studies {30051969; 32222718; 34319004}. Prospective studies are strongly recommended in this field. bManagement options for patients with lung lesions may depend on a variety of factors, including clinical and imaging characteristics, the site of the lesion, the risk of carcinoma of the lung, local disease prevalence, and the local medical infrastructure available. Some clinical management suggestions are outlined above.

Recommendations:

1. Whenever an FNAB result is received, correlation with clinical, imaging, and microbiological findings is mandatory; in patients suspected of having a malignancy, this will be carried out in a multidisciplinary meeting.

2. Whenever an “Atypical” or “Suspicious for malignancy” report is provided, or whenever there is discrepancy between the clinical, imaging, and microbiological findings and the cytopathology report, the reporting cytopathologist should get a second expert opinion on the cytopathology.

3. Routine follow-up at 3–6 months for “Benign” and “Atypical” reports is determined by the patient’s lung cancer risk.

4. ROSE is recommended at transthoracic FNAB and endobronchial ultrasound–guided FNAB.

5. CT or ultrasound is recommended at transthoracic FNAB.
